In [[classical mechanics]], the [[rotation]] of a [[rigid body]] such as a [[spinning top]] under the influence of [[gravity]] is not, in general, an [[integrable problem]]. There are however three famous cases that are integrable, the '''Euler''', the '''Lagrange''', and the '''Kovalevskaya top''', which are in fact the only integrable cases when the system is subject to [[holonomic constraints]].<ref name = "Audin">{{citation
|last=Audin|first=Michèle
|authorlink=Michèle Audin|year=1996
|title=Spinning Tops: A Course on Integrable Systems
|location= New York|publisher= [[Cambridge University Press]] 
| isbn=9780521779197}}.</ref><ref>[[E. T. Whittaker|Whittaker, E. T.]] (1952). 
''[[A Treatise on the Analytical Dynamics of Particles and Rigid Bodies]]''. 
Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521358835}}.</ref><ref>{{cite book 
|last=Strogatz |first=Steven 
|date= 2019
|title= Infinite Powers
|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=rDJoDwAAQBAJ 
|location= New York |publisher= Houghton Mifflin Harcourt 
|page= 287 |isbn= 978-1786492968 |quote= More importantly she [Sofja Wassiljewna Kowalewskaja] proved that no other solvable tops could exist. She had found the last one}}</ref> 
In addition to the energy, each of these tops involves two additional [[constant of motion|constants of motion]] that give rise to the [[Integrable system#Hamiltonian systems and Liouville integrability|integrability]]. 

The Euler top describes a free top without any particular symmetry moving in the absence of any external [[torque]], and for which the fixed point is the [[center of gravity]]. The Lagrange top is a symmetric top, in which two moments of [[inertia]] are the same and the center of gravity lies on the [[symmetry axis]]. The Kovalevskaya top<ref name ="kovalevskaya">{{citation|first=Sofia|last= Kovalevskaya| authorlink=Sofia Kovalevskaya |year=1889| title=Sur le problème de la rotation d'un corps solide autour d'un point fixe|url=https://projecteuclid.org/download/pdf_1/euclid.acta/1485881703|journal=[[Acta Mathematica]]|volume= 12|pages=177–232|language=fr}}</ref><ref>{{cite arxiv
 |last=Kovalevskaya
 |first=Sofia
 |authorlink=Sofia Kovalevskaya
 |title=English translation of Sophie Kowalevski's 'On the problem of the rotation of a rigid body about a fixed point'
 |eprint=2603.07154
 |year=2026
 |class=math.HO
}}</ref><ref name = "Perelemov">Perelemov, A. M. (2002). ''Teoret. Mat. Fiz.'', Volume 131, Number 2, pp. 197–205. {{in lang|fr}}</ref> is a special symmetric top with a unique ratio of the [[Moment_of_inertia|moments of inertia]] which satisfy the relation

: <math> I_1=I_2= 2 I_3,</math>

That is, two moments of inertia are equal, the third is half as large, and the center of gravity is located in the [[plane (geometry)|plane]] perpendicular to the symmetry axis (parallel to the plane of the two degenerate principal axes). 

==Hamiltonian formulation of classical tops==

The configuration of a classical top<ref name="Goldstein">[[Herbert Goldstein]], 
Charles P. Poole, and John L. Safko (2002). ''Classical Mechanics'' (3rd Edition), Addison-Wesley. {{ISBN|9780201657029}}.</ref> is described at time <math>t</math> by three time-dependent [[principal axis (mechanics)|principal axes]], defined by the three [[orthogonal]] vectors <math> \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1</math>, <math> \hat {\mathbf{e}}^2</math> and  <math> \hat{\mathbf{e}}^3</math> with corresponding moments of inertia <math>I_1</math>, <math> I_2</math> and <math>I_3</math> and the [[angular velocity]] about those axes. In a [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian]] formulation of classical tops, the [[conjugate variable|conjugate dynamical variables]] are the components of the [[angular momentum]] vector <math>\bf{L}</math> along the principal axes

: <math>(\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3)= (\mathbf{L}\cdot \hat {\bf{e}}^1,\bf{L}\cdot \hat {\mathbf{e}}^2,\bf{L}\cdot \hat {\mathbf{e}}^3) </math>

and the ''z''-components of the three principal axes, 

: <math>(n_1, n_2, n_3)= (\mathbf{\hat{z}}\cdot \hat {\mathbf{e}}^1,\mathbf{\hat{z}}\cdot \hat {\mathbf{e}}^2,\mathbf{\hat{z}}\cdot \hat {\mathbf{e}}^3) </math>

The [[Poisson bracket]] relations of these variables is given by

: <math>
\{ \ell_a, \ell_b\} = \varepsilon_{abc} \ell_c, \  \{\ell_a, n_b\} = \varepsilon_{abc} n_c, \ \{n_a, n_b\} = 0
</math>

If the position of the center of mass is given by <math> \vec{R}_{cm} = (a \mathbf{\hat e}^1 + b \mathbf{\hat e}^2 + c\mathbf{\hat e}^3)</math>, then the Hamiltonian of a top is given by

: <math> 
H = \frac{(\ell_1)^2}{2I_1}+\frac{(\ell_2)^2}{2I_2}+\frac{(\ell_3)^2}{2I_3} + mg (a n_1 + bn_2 + cn_3) = \frac{(\ell_1)^2}{2I_1}+\frac{(\ell_2)^2}{2I_2}+\frac{(\ell_3)^2}{2I_3} + mg \vec{R}_{cm}\cdot \mathbf{\hat{z}},
</math>

The equations of motion are then determined by

: <math>
\dot{\ell}_a = \{ H, \ell_a\}, \dot{n}_a = \{H, n_a\}.
</math>
Explicitly, these are
<math display = block> \dot \ell_1 = \left(\frac{1}{I_3} - \frac{1}{I_2}\right)\ell_2 \ell_3 + mg(c n_2 - b n_3) </math>
<math display = block> \dot n_1 = \frac{\ell_3}{I_3} n_2 - \frac{\ell_2}{I_2} n_3 </math>
and cyclic permutations of the indices.

=== Mathematical description of phase space ===
In mathematical terms, the spatial configuration of the body is described by a point on the [[Lie group]] <math>SO(3)</math>, the three-dimensional [[rotation group]], which is the rotation matrix from the lab frame to the body frame. The full configuration space or phase space is the [[cotangent bundle]] <math>T^*SO(3)</math>, with the fibers <math>T^*_RSO(3)</math> parametrizing the angular momentum at spatial configuration <math>R</math>. The Hamiltonian is a function on this phase space.

==Euler top==

The Euler top, named after [[Leonhard Euler]], is an untorqued top (for example, a top in free fall), with Hamiltonian

: <math> 
H_{\rm E} = \frac{(\ell_1)^2}{2I_1}+\frac{(\ell_2)^2}{2I_2}+\frac{(\ell_3)^2}{2I_3},
</math>

The four constants of motion are the energy <math>H_{\rm E}</math> and the three components of angular momentum  in the lab frame,

: <math>
(L_1,L_2,L_3) = \ell_1 \mathbf{\hat e}^1 +\ell_2\mathbf{\hat e}^2+ \ell_3 \mathbf{\hat e}^3.
</math>

==Lagrange top==

The Lagrange top,<ref>{{citation|last1=Cushman|first1=R.H.|title=Global Aspects of Classical Integrable Systems|pages=187–270|year=1997|contribution=The Lagrange top|location=Basel|publisher=Birkhäuser|doi=10.1007/978-3-0348-8891-2_5|isbn=978-3-0348-9817-1|last2=Bates|first2=L.M.}}.</ref> named after [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange]], is a symmetric top with the center of mass along the symmetry axis at location, <math> \mathbf{R}_{\rm cm} = h\mathbf{\hat e}^3</math>, with Hamiltonian

: <math> 
H_{\rm L}= \frac{(\ell_1)^2+(\ell_2)^2}{2I}+\frac{(\ell_3)^2}{2I_3}+ mgh n_3.
</math>

The four constants of motion are the energy <math> H_{\rm L}</math>, the angular momentum component along the symmetry axis, <math> \ell_3</math>, the angular momentum in the ''z''-direction

: <math>
L_z = \ell_1n_1+\ell_2n_2+\ell_3n_3,
</math>

and the magnitude of the ''n''-vector 

: <math>
n^2 = n_1^2 + n_2^2 + n_3^2
</math>

==Kovalevskaya top==

The Kovalevskaya top<ref name = "kovalevskaya"/><ref name = "Perelemov"/> is a symmetric top in which <math> I_1=I_2=2I </math>, <math>I_3=I</math> and the center of mass lies in the plane perpendicular to the symmetry axis <math>\mathbf {R}_{\rm cm} = h \mathbf{\hat e}^1</math>. It was discovered by [[Sofia Kovalevskaya]] in 1888 and presented in her paper "Sur le problème de la rotation d'un corps solide autour d'un point fixe", which won her the Prix Bordin from the [[French Academy of Sciences]] in 1888. The Hamiltonian is

: <math>
H_{\rm K}= \frac{(\ell_1)^2+(\ell_2)^2+ 2 (\ell_3)^2}{2I}+ mgh n_1.
</math>

The four constants of motion are the energy <math> H_{\rm K}</math>,  the Kovalevskaya invariant

:<math>
K = \xi_+ \xi_-
</math>

where the variables <math>\xi_\pm</math> are defined by

: <math>
\xi_\pm = (\ell_1\pm i \ell_2 )^2- 2 mgh I(n_1\pm i n_2),
</math>

the angular momentum component in the ''z''-direction,

: <math>
L_z = \ell_1n_1+\ell_2n_2+\ell_3n_3,
</math>

and the magnitude of the ''n''-vector

: <math>
n^2 = n_1^2 + n_2^2 + n_3^2.
</math>

==Nonholonomic constraints==
If the constraints are relaxed to allow [[nonholonomic system|nonholonomic]] constraints, there are other possible integrable tops besides the three well-known cases. The nonholonomic '''Goryachev–Chaplygin top''' (introduced by D. Goryachev in 1900<ref>Goryachev, D. (1900). "On the motion of a rigid material body about a fixed point in the case A = B = C", ''Mat. Sb.'', 21. {{in lang|ru}}. Cited in Bechlivanidis & van Moerbek (1987) and Hazewinkel (2012).</ref> and integrated by [[Sergey Chaplygin]] in 1948<ref>Chaplygin, S.A. (1948). "A new case of rotation of a rigid body, supported at one point", ''Collected Works'', Vol. I, pp. 118–124. Moscow: Gostekhizdat. {{in lang|ru}}. Cited in Bechlivanidis & van Moerbek (1987) and Hazewinkel (2012).</ref><ref>{{citation|last1=Bechlivanidis|first1= C.|last2= van Moerbek|first2= P. |year=1987|url=https://projecteuclid.org/download/pdf_1/euclid.cmp/1104159242|title= The Goryachev–Chaplygin Top and the Toda Lattice| journal=[[Communications in Mathematical Physics]] |volume=110|issue= 2|pages= 317–324|bibcode=1987CMaPh.110..317B|doi=10.1007/BF01207371|s2cid= 119927045}}</ref>) is also integrable (<math>I_1=I_2=4I_3</math>). Its center of gravity lies in the [[equatorial plane]].<ref>[[Michiel Hazewinkel|Hazewinkel, Michiel]]; ed. (2012). ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=RhD8CAAAQBAJ&q=goryachev-chaplygin+top&pg=PA271 Encyclopaedia of Mathematics]'', pp. 271–2. Springer. {{ISBN|9789401512886}}.
</ref>
